submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole is a retrospective detector for everyday interpersonal exchange: it fires on the ordinary verbs of people dealing with one another - talk, chat, help, share, thank, agree, offer, advise - and on the speaker or addressee words that frame them (I, me, my, us, your; the peak sits on ' your' in 'thank you for your help' and on ' my' in 'I helped my sister'), landing on whichever of those words closes the social phrase, and most strongly when the speaker or addressee is a participant. It stays at the floor for the same events rendered as a solitary action on an object (read, work, watch, keep, eat), in a formal or institutional register (assisted, greeted, 'the committee agreed to the plan'), and for formulaic arithmetic and code; the negative pole is the impersonal end of that axis, most suppressed on formulaic math such as 'greatest common divisor'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Apiary management summary, March to October

Hive inspections were carried out at seven-day intervals from the middle of March until the end of September. Each colony was opened on the warmest dry afternoon of the week, and every brood frame was lifted and examined for signs of disease. Findings were written into a field notebook and later transcribed into a spreadsheet kept in the shed.

Varroa pressure was monitored using sticky boards placed under the brood chamber and checked at every inspection. The threshold was set at three mites per day. Above that level, oxalic acid was applied by vaporiser. Mite counts fell sharply during the fortnight after treatment and then recovered slowly through the autumn.

Queen status was recorded at each visit. In two colonies the old queen was replaced after supersedure cells appeared along the lower edge of the comb. Replacement queens were reared at a nearby apiary and introduced inside a small cage plugged at one end. Acceptance was confirmed when fresh eggs were seen on the following inspection.

Honey stores were weighed at the start of every month. The spring flow was weak, and sugar syrup was given to four colonies during a dry spell in June. The main flow began in the second week of July and continued into early August. Supers were added whenever the combs were drawn out. Extraction took place in the first week of September, and the crop was filtered and bottled in the shed.

Wax cappings were rinsed, melted in a slow cooker and poured into moulds. The resulting blocks were stored in paper and labelled by season. Equipment was scraped, flamed and stacked on shelves according to size. Smokers were emptied after each visit, and the bellows were checked for cracks. Veils were washed at the end of the month and hung to dry.

Disease checks followed the standard schedule. Samples of adult bees were sent to the regional laboratory in July. The results came back clear for both foulbrood and nosema. A single frame of chalkbrood was removed from the weakest colony and burned. The hive was requeened in August, and the colony built up again before the cold weather arrived.

Weather records were kept alongside the hive notes. Rainfall for the season was below average, and the three hottest days in July were noted. Wind direction was recorded because two hives sit at the exposed corner of the field. A windbreak of hazel hurdles was erected in the spring and held up well.

Records from the previous three seasons were compared. Yields per hive were slightly below the five-year average, largely because of the dry June. The pattern matched the district figures circulated in the autumn bulletin.

Winter preparation began in the last week of September. Entrances were narrowed, mouse guards were fitted, and every hive was strapped down against gales. Insulation boards were placed under the roofs. The final inspection was completed on the twenty-eighth of October. The apiary was then left undisturbed until the following spring.

Expenses were tallied at the end of the season. Jar lids, labels and foundation accounted for most of the outlay. Sales were handled at the village market on Saturday mornings, and the accounts were balanced before Christmas.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long third-person apiary report on the same topic as example 1 but with no first- or second-person frame and no exchange verb, testing whether the original activation came from the beekeeping topic rather than interpersonal exchange.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Ruth had not been back to the house in eleven years. The lane still narrowed at the same bend, and the gate still scraped the same flagstone. She sat in the car for a minute before she got out, watching the curtain twitch.

She had brought nothing. She had meant to stop at the services and buy flowers, or wine, or something wrapped in cellophane, but the rain had been heavy and the exit came up quickly and she had driven past it.

Her aunt was at the sink when she came in, sleeves pushed past the elbow, and for a moment did not turn around. The kitchen smelled of onions and old wood. On the dresser the photographs had been rearranged. There were new ones of children Ruth had never met, and one of her uncle in a suit she did not recognise.

They ate at the small table by the window. Margaret asked about the motorway and the state of the roads, and Ruth described the drive in detail: the roadworks near Birmingham, the service station where the coffee had gone cold. Margaret said the same roadworks had delayed the bus for forty minutes on Tuesday. Neither of them mentioned the eleven years.

After the plates were cleared, Margaret brought out a tin of shortbread and a pot of tea. She asked about Ruth's work, and Ruth explained the new office, the woman in accounts who had left without notice, the manager who never answered emails. Margaret listened and said that offices had been the same when she was young, and that a good secretary was worth two managers. Ruth laughed and said that there were no secretaries any more.

The light went orange and then grey. Margaret switched on the lamp above the dresser. Ruth carried the plates to the sink without being asked and offered to wash up. Margaret thanked her and said she should not have bothered. Ruth said it was the least she could do.

They washed up together, Ruth in the soapy water and Margaret at her shoulder drying the same plate twice. Ruth handed over the cups one at a time. Margaret asked whether Ruth would come again in the summer, for the fete, and Ruth said she would. She meant it.

Before she left she walked down the garden. The apple tree had been cut back hard and the shed had a new roof. The bean rows were tidy, and a plastic chair still stood where her uncle used to sit.

On her way out she stopped in the hall and thanked her aunt for keeping the photographs out. Margaret waved the thanks away and said that the house had been too quiet for too long.

The gate scraped behind her. She drove home in the dark, and for the first hour did not turn on the radio.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long fiction passage in which the exchange verbs and frame words appear only deep in the document, testing that the claimed feature fires in long context and in a genre unlike the examples.
